Newly hatched Northern wolffish larvae measure approximately 2 cm [Lb = approximately 2 cm] in total length, a relatively modest size at birth for this large-bodied anarhichadid species. During the initial weeks post-eclosion, these endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves while undergoing progressive yolk utilization. The yolk sac is typically resorbed when the larva reaches about 20 mm, marking the transition to first exogenous feeding. In the congeneric species Anarhichas lupus and Anarhichas minor, complete absorption of yolk nutrients also occurs at roughly 20 mm, suggesting a conserved developmental pattern within the genus. Following the trophic switch to active feeding, larval growth proceeds rapidly as these planktonic individuals disperse into the water column. The subsequent larval-juvenile transition involves a profound morphological transformation, including the development of the characteristic robust dentition and benthic orientation that defines the adult form of Anarhichas denticulatus.

Eggs of the Northern wolffish require an incubation period of approximately 10 months [ab = approximately 10 months] before eclosion occurs when maintained at a stable water temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], consistent with the extended embryogenesis typical of cold-water marine teleosts. This protracted developmental duration, nearly a full year, reflects the slow metabolic rates imposed by the frigid conditions of the species' deepwater habitat. Field records indicate that females deposit large, demersal, adhesive eggs in rocky crevices where the male remains on guard throughout the incubation period. The yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion with a prominent yolk sac that sustains the individual through the initial non-feeding stage. Experimental evidence from captive rearing programs supports the finding that hatching success is highest within the temperature window of 2 to 5 °C, with developmental rates slowing noticeably at the lower end of this thermal range. Ultimately, the age at birth for this species is comparable to that documented for other long-lived, slow-maturing members of the Anarhichadidae family.

Female Northern wolffish achieve sexual maturity and begin gametogenesis at approximately 6 to 8 years of age, with first reproduction occurring at around 6 years after hatching [tR = around 6 years after hatching] when maintained at a water temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. This delayed maturation is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy adapted to the stable but resource-limited environment of the North Atlantic continental slope. The onset of reproductive activity is accompanied by vitellogenesis and an increase in gonad mass as females prepare for their first spawning season. Spawning adults typically produce large, yolky eggs that are deposited in rocky substrate nests. Annual reproductive output is substantial; females produce approximately 116 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 116 eggs per day] during the peak spawning period, a rate that reflects the considerable energetic investment required for offspring production in this cold-water species. The combination of late age at first breeding and high fecundity per spawning event underscores an iteroparous reproductive strategy in which adults invest heavily in each reproductive bout while spreading reproductive effort across multiple years.

The total length at which female Northern wolffish attain puberty and become capable of spawning is approximately 80 cm [Lp = approximately 80 cm], a size threshold that typically corresponds to the 6 to 8 year age range reported for this species. This length at puberty represents a substantial portion of the ultimate total length the species can achieve, suggesting that individuals must invest considerable time in somatic growth before reproductive maturation begins. Upon reaching this size, gonadal recrudescence proceeds through the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, leading to the production of mature gametes. The largest documented individuals of Anarhichas denticulatus reach a maximum total length of 138 cm [Li = 138 cm], a size attained only after many years of sustained growth in the cold, productive waters of their boreal range. Adult wet weight also scales substantially with length; the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown specimen can reach 32,000 grams [Wwi = 32,000 grams], representing a considerable increase from the 2 cm length at birth. This dramatic growth trajectory highlights the species' capacity for extensive somatic investment over its long lifespan.

Longevity data from otolith-based age estimates indicate that Northern wolffish can survive for at least 16 years [am = at least 16 years] in their natural environment when maintained at a temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], positioning this species among the longer-lived members of the North Atlantic demersal fish community. This extended lifespan, coupled with the late age at first reproduction and high fecundity, aligns with a life-history strategy adapted to environments where juvenile survival is unpredictable but adult mortality remains relatively low. The maximum recorded reproductive rate is approximately 116 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 116 eggs per day] during the spawning season, a sustained output that requires substantial lipid reserves accumulated over the non-reproductive period. Senescence in this species is gradual, with reproductively viable adults continuing to spawn well into their second decade of life. The combination of a decade-and-a-half lifespan, delayed maturation at 80 cm total length at puberty, and substantial asymptotic mass of 32,000 grams positions the Northern wolffish as a classic K-selected predator within its cold-water ecosystem.
